title: Chulalongkorn Researchers Call for Greater Quantum Investment in Thailand
html:
Insider Brief

  • Chulalongkorn University researchers are calling for sustained investment in quantum education and research to prepare Thailand for opportunities in quantum computing, industry and data security.
  • The researchers say Thailand could enter the quantum industry by developing specialist components and expertise in areas such as quantum sensing and communications.
  • They also recommend that organisations review their encryption systems and prepare for post-quantum cryptography as quantum computing advances.

PRESS RELEASE — Chulalongkorn University physicists are urging Thailand to build quantum expertise and
strengthen research support to prepare for opportunities in computing, industry and data security. With specialists taking years to train, the university’s learning programs offer a way to start preparing now.

Assistant Professor Dr. Thiparat Chotibut, Assistant Professor Dr. Salinporn Kittiwatanakul and Dr. Supanut Thanasilp, of Chula’s Department of Physics, Faculty of Science, said preparation should begin before quantum computing becomes widely available. Chula’s Siam Quantum Square (SQ²) offers educational activities and free online courses for students and the public.

Thailand began developing a national quantum technology roadmap in 2017–2018, with initial research funding following in 2020. The researchers emphasized that sustained investment in knowledge and people would help the country participate in emerging industries.

Dr. Thiparat said Thailand need not build an entire quantum computer to compete with major technological powers. Developing specific components or specialized expertise could offer a route into the industry’s supply chain. Experience in quantum sensing and communication, which share some of the same underlying principles, could also lay the groundwork for advances in computing.

Quantum computing uses quantum bits, or qubits, to process information differently from conventional computers. Potential applications include molecular simulations for drug and materials development, investment portfolio optimization and energy resource allocation. However, the technology remains under development. Hardware costs, qubit reliability, computational errors and the need to identify suitable applications continue to limit practical use. Quantum computers are expected to complement conventional processors, with each
handling tasks suited to its capabilities.

Security preparation is another priority. Dr. Salinporn said sufficiently powerful quantum computers could threaten RSA encryption by solving the mathematical problems underpinning its protection. “A quantum computer is like a sword, but we also need to develop a shield to protect ourselves,” she said.

That protection is being developed through approaches such as post-quantum cryptography, designed to withstand attacks from quantum computers, and quantum key distribution, which can help detect eavesdropping during the exchange of encryption keys. Dr. Supanut urged organizations to review their encryption and plan upgrades, especially for data that must remain confidential for years.

Through education and research, Chula can help Thailand develop the expertise to make informed decisions about quantum technology—from protecting sensitive data to identifying applications that could benefit local industries.

Mohib Ur Rehman

MENTIONED IN THE ARTICLE

Chulalongkorn University is an autonomous public research university located in Bangkok, Thailand, and is the oldest institution of higher education in the country, established as a national university in 1917. It is a comprehensive institution conducting research across health sciences, social sciences, engineering, and science & technology, with interdisciplinary strengths in quantum technology, artificial intelligence, advanced materials, and computer science. In the quantum sector, it operates the flagship Siam Quantum Square (SQ2) initiative, installed Southeast Asia's first trapped-ion quantum computer through international joint laboratories (including with USTC and Hefei Unitary Quantum Technology), offers a Master of Science in Quantum Technology program, and conducts research on superconducting qubits, quantum algorithms, quantum machine learning, and continuous quantum measurement techniques.
